newsitem.title: CROATIA: Father of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, takes his vows.
newsitem.headline: Father of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman, takes his vows.

text.p: President Franjo Tudjman, the man who built Croatia out of the ruins of the Yugoslav war, was sworn in on Tuesday for five more years in which he will try to realise Croatia's dream of finally joining Western Europe.

The man who led his country in a war against Serbs in 1991 now faces the task of convincing his countrymen, as well as foreign powers, that the time has come to heal the wounds of war and move once and for all towards the West.
But diplomats say he will have to substitute action for words if he wants to achieve this.

The hangover of war is slow to clear, with demands from the West for Tudjman to use his influence to turn over Bosnian Croat war criminals hiding out in Bosnia, let Serb refugees return home and release his iron grip on the state media.

He is reported to be suffering from cancer yet he looked fitter at the start of his new term of office than he had for some time. The trademark shock of white hair which won him sympathy last year as it thinned, looks thicker and shinier and the gaunt face is beginning to look rounder.
His medical team say he is fit and even Western diplomats admit to being surprised at the evident recovery. Under Croatian law this will be his last term as president.

A slight, charismatic politician with a penchant for wearing a white military uniform bedecked with medals when inspecting troops on national days, Tudjman has emulated his mentor Josip Broz Tito, partisan and later communist Yugoslav leader.

After proclaiming Croatian independence for the first time since 1102, he has been hailed as the "Father of the Nation" and his popularity remains strong despite criticism at home and abroad in later years.
He was accused of plotting with then-Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic to split Bosnia in two during the war and form a greater Serbia and a greater Croatia.
However he later won praise from the West for signing the Dayton peace treaty which ended the war in 1995.
His critics recently returned to berate him for failing to meet commitments he made in that treaty, especially his control of the media and failure to stop attacks on minority Serbs.

In 1989 he formed the Croatian Democratic Union which set its sights on Croatian independence as Yugoslavia fell apart and Communism died across eastern Europe. His party defeated the communists in the first free democratic vote in 1990.

During his first full presidential term after being elected president of independent Croatia in August 1992, Tudjman had to face accusations of corruption in his party and criticism of his autocratic style. Those complaints are as strong as ever.

Since the end of the Bosnian war Croatia has been viewed by the United States as a possible stabilising force in the region and diplomats say its role is vital to shore up Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation, a cornerstone of the treaty formed with U.S. diplomacy.
Tudjman's hardline rhetoric delivered to domestic audiences during various tough negotiations, has often been followed by surprise turnarounds along the lines suggested by the West.
But his reluctance to force Bosnian Croats, over whom he still has a strong influence, to hand over indictees to the Hague war crimes tribunal has irritated the West.
Loans have been withheld and Croatia's integration into Western institutions could be blocked if demands are not met.

He will see the last Serb enclave finally come back under Zagreb rule when the United Nations mission which has run the region since January 1996 ends next January. Around half of the 100,000 Serbs who live there are expected to go back to their pre-war homes, and the rest to leave for Serbia.
Some however will stay, and the integration of them with thousands of Croats going back home will be closely watched.
